title: Kim Thomson & Alan Weedon - Breaking and Entering
summary: Kim Thomson & Alan Weedon on Breaking and Entering
transcript:
Swampland managing editor Kimberley Thomson and creative director Alan Weedon joined Lauren Taylor and Simon Winkler in the Triple R studio on 21 June 2018 to discuss the magazine's fourth issue, long-form music journalism and their beginnings at Voiceworks. The issue was to be launched at the Gasometer Hotel on 29 June. Edited for length and clarity.

Lauren: Swampland was founded as a forum for long-form music journalism, something that's not always given space online. Apparently the idea arrived when you were staring at another best-of clickbait list. At what point did you realise the dream of Swampland would become a reality?

Kim: I was thinking about this today, actually, and it's been almost two years exactly since we first conceptualised the idea. That best-of list was actually in Rolling Stone, so it was in another print magazine. It was something like the 40 greatest punk albums of all time, and it was the Ramones and the usual suspects, a lot of what would now be old men. That kind of twigged something in my brain. I was like, I want to buy this magazine, but it's not giving me what I want to read. It's very outdated, and they're just going to keep producing the same thing ad infinitum, basically.

Alan: It's interesting now, in 2018, you've seen publications like Pitchfork apologise for the way they used to numerically put somebody's three years or a year's worth of work into this arbitrary number, and the way they used to hold so much influence over how people conceived of what good music was. Journalism has flipped on its head, and it doesn't know what it is anymore. But you've also got players like Pitchfork still in the field, owned by Condé Nast, who now do The New Yorker and Vogue. In Australia that context is a lot smaller. Rolling Stone Australia is now broke, so it's a fun time to be in publishing.

Simon: The editorial spectrum of some of those magazines was very narrow, with a reductive quality to a lot of content presented in a digital era. Swampland privileges a more in-depth analysis and a broader scope. Kim, in a feature in magCulture, you talked about Australia being an incredibly diverse country, but a small number of stories having been focused on for a long time. Can you talk about the more inclusive editorial policy underpinning Swampland?

Kim: I don't think we really started off thinking about that, but it evolved naturally. The people making the most interesting music in the country, at least in my opinion at the moment, are people who have been traditionally marginalised or not centred in the narrative of what Australian music is. I think we're at a particularly interesting time where we're having conversations about who is making the music and the power structures that have existed. That sort of just happened. The artists we've focused on maybe wouldn't have appeared in Rolling Stone or traditional media outlets. I think it's just a natural thing to have occurred.

Alan: It also comes at a time when a lot of arts pages and mainstream publications have been completely curtailed. The way music or arts journalism functions is a lot more precarious, in the sense that there's less space to be constructively critical, if that makes sense, because everybody is responding to a presser that was due yesterday.

Lauren: Can you share the process of putting together each issue? Kimberley, where does it start for you?

Kim: That's a good question. How does it start? Alan, do you want to take that one as creative director? It's all a blur in my mind.

Alan: The editorial cycle is never quite the same. Essentially, for us, it's stories that excite us or stories that have been particularly underrepresented. It also follows the music we consume. If we've been to a good gig or we're listening to somebody at the moment, Sampa the Great is somebody we had on our minds since issue one, basically. We also come at a nexus of writing and music. Both Kim and I study journalism, and we're fond of amazing writing, so Maxine Beneba Clarke was our dream candidate. We thought it would be an interesting way to frame the issue. To cycle back and answer your question, it's going out and talking to friends and peers, reading, consuming the ideas and information out there and trying to synthesise what else could be said that would be considered, as opposed to a hack job.

Kim: We throw out a lot of ideas initially, chuck stuff at the wall and see what sticks. We have a long list of things that maybe don't happen, and sometimes they work out for the best, like the Sampa and Maxine piece. We also accept pitches and outside submissions, so we get quite a few stories that way as well. But it is a really lengthy process. It takes us six months to put an issue together, and we're thinking beyond that as well. Print is quite an intense process.

Alan: When you're thinking in a print context, one thing we think about as editors is that we can't rely on perpetual editability. We can't save a new draft or republish a website. The print, that's it for eternity, essentially, if paper lasts that long. It's interesting to think about how the stories are designed to transcend ageing. They have to be standalone pieces that can't just be within a given quarter.

Simon: You were saying before, Kim, that this wasn't necessarily front of mind when you started, but Swampland has evolved to become a chronicle of changes in Australian and international music. Would that be fair to say?

Kim: I think so, and also culturally, outside of music. I was reading back through my editor's letters in previous issues, and in passing I mentioned things that had been happening. We started in 2016, which was a pretty strange year for a lot of reasons. We were going to press as Donald Trump was becoming president, or the election was just about to happen. I think they do act as a timestamp of these six-month blocks, and so much has happened within a relatively short space of time. One of the aims of the magazine is to document stuff as it happens, and hopefully people will read back over it in the future.

Simon: Your editorial brief is very broad. Are you sometimes surprised by connections you find when looking over the issue, things you might not have seen at the start but that become amplified as you go?

Kim: That actually happens every issue, I think. Maybe it's a matter of Australian music being quite small in some ways. In this particular issue we have a story on Little Ugly Girls, this amazing band from Hobart in the '90s. I wrote a piece on Tom Lyngcoln from The Nation Blue, and he talks about how Little Ugly Girls were a massive influence on him. They were coming out of the Hobart scene at similar times. We weren't thinking about that carrying through the issue, but the pieces speak to each other, and that's happened in previous issues too, hasn't it?

Alan: The pieces do speak to each other, but it's also interesting how certain stories pan out and there are glimpses of things you wouldn't necessarily get if somebody did a short, 500-word interview on a release. In this issue we've got a feature with UV boi, and there's this beautiful anecdote where he was in Newcastle at a gig. In the space of a paragraph, it's revealed that he was at Domino's trying to get food, and the guy who served him was Mall Grab. This is when Mall Grab was just some kid in Newcastle. By the end of the article, there's this portrait of Mall Grab and UV boi meeting again and Mall Grab saying, you're the reason I got into music. I thought it was a beautiful insight that I otherwise would never have known about if we didn't give space to have these stories told.

Lauren: I wanted to ask about your relationship with magazines growing up. Did you spend a lot of time at the newsagent, the library or supermarkets browsing?

Alan: Yes, many hours. When we were looking at that magCulture feature that had Kim interviewed, we bonded over the fact that we really loved K-Zone, the kids' magazine.

Kim: That's where it all began, I think.

Alan: I was very jealous of my friends who got illustrations published by them, because I wanted to be published.

Simon: Did you hoard magazines and drag them from house to house?

Kim: I still do.

Alan: I do. It's a bit of an issue, pardon the pun.

Kim: A big one for me is NME. Maybe that's where I got the idea of starting a music magazine, but I religiously read NME when I was in high school.

Alan: Same for me. I would call bookshops and be like, hello, do you have Rolling Stone America? Is it in yet? Can you reserve it for me? I'd make sure it was there at a certain point in time. My poor mother, she's still probably got shelves filled with my back issues of Rolling Stone Australia. For a while I had a phase where I read Clash, an amazing print music journal from the UK. We've been cyclical, in a sense. Small-press print publications are thriving again. There are newer players I pick up from time to time, like Record magazine. It's quite good as well.

Kim: We also met through a different magazine, or literary journal, Voiceworks, which is a lit journal for Australian writers and editors under the age of 25. Me and Alan were both non-fiction editors there. The other member of our core team, Kelsey Oldham, was also a non-fiction editor there. She's the deputy editor of Swampland. That's how we learnt the skills to put a print magazine together, really.

Alan: It was an amazing opportunity, because we still work with people we worked with at Voiceworks. Sinéad Stubbins, for example, is somebody I edited at Voiceworks when she was talking about the political importance of the cheeseburger. She was in our first issue, and I'm sure there are other writers we could think of.

Kim: Anwen Crawford, I'm pretty sure, started at Voiceworks — had work in Voiceworks. Ben Law. Anna Krien as well.

Alan: It's still going strong. If you're under 25, look it up. And they pay you.
